newsitem.title: USA: Sharp fall in stocks pushes dollar broadly lower.
newsitem.headline: Sharp fall in stocks pushes dollar broadly lower.

text.p: The dollar ended modestly lower against the German mark and the Japanese yen Monday, unable to overcome a second consecutive sharp drop in Wall Street stocks.
On the heels of Thursday's 140-point tumble, the Dow Jones industrial average fell 157.11 points Monday to 6,583.48, its seventh-largest point drop ever.
The dollar followed suit, moving in lockstep with stocks for much of the day, though ultimately rebounding to end up from early session lows.

"The stock market weighed on the dollar very heavily," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole. "I think everybody was expecting more stock market weakness and we got it."
The dollar settled at 1.6750 marks, down from 1.6800 at Thursday's close, after briefly touching a near two-month low of 1.6615 marks in morning trade.
Against the yen, the dollar ended modestly weaker at 123.78, down from 124.10 Thursday.
Markets were closed Friday for observance of Good Friday.
Still reeling from the Federal Reserve's decision to hike U.S. official interest rates last Tuesday, stocks were pummeled Monday.

A series of economic releases, including personal income and consumption data, showed ample strength in the U.S. economy, fuelling expectations that the Federal Reserve could push official interest rates even higher in the months ahead.
The Commerce Department reported that U.S. incomes jumped 0.9 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $6.71 trillion in February -- the fastest rate of increase in eight months.
While higher rates are often supportive of the dollar, dealers seized on weakness in U.S. stocks Monday as a reason to sell the currency.

"The expectations of higher rates are not positive for the dollar right now because of their impact on the asset markets, in particular the stock market," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co. of New York.
Traders said the Easter holiday, which kept foreign exchange desks closed throughout Europe, may have been partly responsible for Monday's roller-coaster price fluctuations.
When trading volume is below normal levels, currency movements tend to become magnified.
"The volumes were not normal and as such movement may have been exaggerated," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan.
In other trade on Monday, the dollar ended lower at 1.4485 Swiss francs, down from 1.4512 late Thursday. The British pound rose to $1.6395 from $1.6310.
The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3845 from C$1.3806 on Thursday.
